props.title: Super Size Me

sections.content: Super Size Me revolutionized food documentaries by turning director Morgan Spurlock into a human guinea pig. His 30-day McDonald's-only diet experiment exposed fast food's health impacts with shocking personal consequences - gaining 24 pounds, liver damage, and depression. This sparked a wave of investigative food docs like Food, Inc. (2008) and Fed Up (2014). Spurlock's blend of humor, personal stakes, and hard data created a template for documentary filmmaking that persists today.

sections.content: The cultural impact of Super Size Me was immediate and lasting. McDonald's removed their "Super Size" option within six weeks of the film's release. The documentary triggered a wave of corporate responsibility films like The Corporation (2003) and Walmart: The High Cost of Low Price (2005). These films shared Spurlock's approach of making complex systemic issues personally relatable through compelling narratives and clear villains.

Food documentaries evolved beyond fast food critique. Jiro Dreams of Sushi (2011) celebrated culinary artistry. Chef's Table (2015) turned food docs into visual poetry. That Sugar Film (2014) followed Spurlock's self-experiment format but focused on hidden sugars in "healthy" foods. Each built on Super Size Me's foundation while expanding the genre's scope. sections.content: Super Size Me influenced documentaries beyond food. Films like The True Cost (2015) exposed fast fashion's hidden costs, while Blackfish (2013) challenged SeaWorld's treatment of orcas. Both used Spurlock's technique of making institutional critique personal through individual stories and clear cause-effect relationships.

The film's success also sparked corporate response documentaries. McDonald's funded 540 Meals: Choices Make the Difference (2014) to counter Spurlock's narrative. This pattern of corporate pushback through film continues today, showing Super Size Me's lasting impact on both documentary techniques and corporate PR strategies.
